claims.claim: assert_frame_equal: NaN in the same place is equal; float columns use relative tolerance 1e-5 (1.000005 passes, 1.00002 fails); integers compare exactly; column order, index and dtype differences fail; check_like=True ignores column and row order by label.
np.testing.assert_allclose defaults rtol=1e-07, atol=0, equal_nan=True; 1e-12 against 0.0 fails without atol.

concept_html:
== on DataFrames compares cell by cell and returns another DataFrame. It treats two missing values as different and ignores dtypes. Use the pandas testing helpers instead. In pandas 3.0, pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, expected) checks:

  • values, with missing values in the same place counted as equal,
  • dtypes, so a count that silently became float fails,
  • column names and their order,
  • the index.

Float columns are compared with a relative tolerance of 1e-5 by default, so 0.1 + 0.2 matches 0.3. Integer columns must match exactly. pd.testing.assert_series_equal does the same for one column.

Two options matter most:

  • check_like=True ignores the order of columns, and of rows with the same index labels.
  • check_dtype=False ignores dtypes. Reach for it rarely: a dtype change is often the bug.

Filtering keeps the original index labels. After df[df["w"] > 0] drops row 1, the index is [0, 2], and a comparison with a freshly built expected frame fails on the index. Decide what the function promises. If it promises a fresh index, it calls .reset_index(drop=True) and the test stays strict.

To compare rows whatever their order, sort both frames by their key columns and reset both indexes before comparing.

For NumPy arrays, use np.testing.assert_allclose(actual, expected). Its defaults are rtol=1e-7 and atol=0, and it treats NaN as equal to NaN. A relative tolerance never accepts any difference from an expected 0, so add atol when an expected value is 0.

Test that a function leaves its input alone. Take before = df.copy(), call the function, then compare df with before. Without .copy(), before is the same object and the comparison can never fail.

def test_drop_zero_weights() -> None:
df = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["R1", "R2", "R3"], "w": [1.0, 0.0, 2.0]})
before = df.copy()
result = drop_zero_weights(df)
expected = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["R1", "R3"], "w": [1.0, 2.0]})
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(result, expected)
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(df, before)

exercises.solution:
import pandas as pd


def assert_same_rows(actual: pd.DataFrame, expected: pd.DataFrame, keys: list[str]) -> None:
    """Assert two frames hold the same rows, ignoring row and column order.

    Args:
        actual: Frame produced by the code under test.
        expected: Frame the test expects.
        keys: Columns that identify a row, used to sort both frames.

    Raises:
        AssertionError: If rows, values or dtypes differ.
    """
    left = actual.sort_values(keys).reset_index(drop=True)
    right = expected.sort_values(keys).reset_index(drop=True)
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(left, right, check_like=True)

title: Testing pandas and NumPy code
why_html: A refactor of a respondent-count function introduced a missing value, so pandas turned the integer n column into float. Every downstream check still compared with == and passed. The report template formatted n with {:,} and printed "1,204.0 respondents" on 40 pages. assert_frame_equal against an expected frame with an int64 column fails on that change.
